citeinfo.title: Sensor data from debris-flow experiments conducted in May, 2017, at the USGS debris-flow flume, HJ Andrews Experimental Forest, Blue River, Oregon

descript.abstract: The files consist of two types: tabulated data files and graphical map files. Data files consist of three .csv files, representing three experiment dates (2017_05_23, 2017_05_24, 2017_05_25). Each of these files contains multiple columns of data, with each column representing either a time measurement or the value of a physical quantity measured at that time (e.g., flow depth, pore pressure, normal stress, etc.). Map files consist of three .pdf files, each representing an experiment date listed above. The maps show the thickness of the sediment deposited onto the runout pad after each experiment. Sediment thickness was determined using photogrammetery software from Agisoft.
descript.purpose: These data were collected as part of a long-term program of large-scale experimentation at the USGS debris-flow flume. The chief focus of the three experiments performed in 2017 and represented in this data set was twofold: (1) measurement of evolving basal stresses as the flume headgate opened, and (2) measurement of broadband seismic energy radiated by the moving debris flows. Seismological data are archived at: https://service.iris.edu/ph5ws/

procstep.procdesc: Measurements of the flume headgate opening rate, debris flow thicknesses, basal normal forces, basal shear forces, and basal pore-fluid pressures were acquired with analog electronic sensors deployed at several locations along the length of the flume. All sensor outputs (voltages) were sampled digitally at 1000 hertz (Hz) with a 14-bit data acquisition system. Empirical calibration factors, which were established for each sensor by repeated testing, were used to translate these voltages to the system of physical units (SI) tabulated here.

overview.eaover: Three .pdf files each illustrate two map views of deposits formed on the runout pad at the foot of the USGS debris-flow flume during experiments conducted in May, 2017. In each file one map view depicts an overhead photograph of the deposit, and the other depicts an isopach map of deposit thicknesses (in meters) constructed photogrammetrically from stereo overhead photographs. Top maps are superposed on an orthorectified background image of the concrete runout pad at the foot of the flume. Black grid lines painted on the runout pad have 1-meter spacing. Scales along the margins of the maps show distances in meters. The numerals on the horizontal axis of each map correspond to local flume control points. The files are listed as 2017_05_23_FC_archive.pdf, 2017_05_24_FC_archive.pdf, 2017_05_25_FC_archive.pdf.
